The Dutch East India Company, or VOC (Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie), was a chartered trading company founded in the Netherlands in 1602 that ruled the spice trade of Asia for nearly two centuries. It was one of the first companies to sell shares to the public, and its shares traded on the Amsterdam Exchange.

The Dutch Republic, at war with Spain and Portugal, merged several rival trading firms into one and gave it a monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia. It also gave the company powers usually held by states: to make war and treaties, build forts, mint coins and govern colonies.

What it did with them:

  • It made Batavia, now Jakarta, its Asian headquarters in 1619, under the governor-general Jan Pieterszoon Coen.
  • It seized the nutmeg islands in the brutal conquest of Banda in 1621, killing or enslaving most of the inhabitants.
  • It took Malacca from Portugal in 1641 and much of Ceylon for its cinnamon.
  • It was the only European trader allowed in Japan, at Dejima in Nagasaki, from 1641.
  • It founded the Cape Colony in South Africa in 1652 as a supply station.

It moved far more ships and people than any rival: nearly a million Europeans sailed to Asia on its ships over its lifetime, many of whom never came back. It also ran a large slave trade within Asia. Competition from the British East India Company, corruption and wars with Britain wore it down. It went bankrupt, and in 1799 the Dutch state took over its debts and its lands, which became the Dutch East Indies.
